content: In 1862, English physician John Langdon Down first identified Down syndrome as a distinct form of intellectual disability. He later published a more detailed report in 1866 titled Observations on an Ethnic Classification of Idiots. Down noted that children with this condition exhibited physical facial features, such as epicanthic folds, which he believed resembled those of individuals from what Blumenbach described as the Mongolian race. Consequently, he used terms like Mongolism and Mongolian idiocy to describe the condition. At the time, idiocy was a medical term used to denote severe intellectual impairment. Down theorized that Mongolism represented a form of regression, suggesting that the appearance of these traits in children of Caucasian parents indicated a reversion to a less advanced racial type. By the early 20th century, Mongolian idiocy had become one of the most recognizable forms of intellectual disability. Most individuals with this condition were institutionalized, and their associated medical issues were rarely treated. As a result, many died in infancy or early adulthood. During the rise of the eugenics movement, several countries, including 33 of the 48 U.S. states, implemented programs of involuntary sterilization targeting individuals with Down syndrome and similar disabilities. The most extreme manifestation of such policies was the German euthanasia program Aktion T-4, initiated in 1940. However, public outrage and legal challenges led to the discontinuation or repeal of these programs after World War II. Over time, even voluntary institutionalization of children with Down syndrome became rare in Western countries. Until the mid-20th century, the cause of Down syndrome remained unknown. Observations had been made regarding its occurrence across all racial groups, its association with advanced maternal age, and the rarity of recurrence within families. Standard medical texts speculated that the condition might result from a combination of unidentified inheritable factors. Some experts also hypothesized that trauma during pregnancy could play a role. The development of karyotyping techniques in the 1950s allowed scientists to identify chromosomal abnormalities. In 1959, Professor Jérôme Lejeune discovered that Down syndrome was caused by the presence of an extra chromosome. This additional chromosome was later identified as the 21st, leading to the condition being named trisomy 21. The numbering of chromosome 21 was based on its size, as it was initially thought to be the second smallest chromosome. Although it was later determined that chromosome 22 is slightly larger than chromosome 21, the established numbering system and the name trisomy 21 were retained to avoid confusion. In 1961, a group of 19 geneticists wrote to the editor of The Lancet, arguing that the term Mongolian idiocy was misleading, outdated, and inappropriate. They proposed that the terminology be changed. The Lancet supported the adoption of the term Down's syndrome. In 1965, the World Health Organization (WHO) officially discontinued the use of Mongolism following a request from the Mongolian delegate. However, the term persisted in some medical texts for decades. In 1975, the United States National Institute of Health convened a conference to standardize the nomenclature of congenital malformations. The conference recommended eliminating the possessive form of eponyms, stating that the possessive use of an eponym should be discontinued, as the author neither had nor owned the disorder. While both Down syndrome and Down's syndrome are used in general discourse, Down syndrome is the preferred term among professionals in the United States, Canada, and other countries, whereas Down's syndrome remains common in the United Kingdom and some other regions.
